title: New atrial fibrillation after surgery

header.contentArea: MRCS Part B • emergency surgical decision-making

related.why: postoperative fluids; both assess reversible postoperative physiology
hyperkalaemia; both assess reversible postoperative physiology

brief.scenario: You are the core surgical trainee on a general surgical ward. A 71-year-old patient on postoperative day 2 after right hemicolectomy has palpitations.
brief.task: Review the ECG, identify risk, and tell the examiner how you would assess and manage the patient.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Treat postoperative AF as a clinical syndrome: assess stability first, ECG-confirm, find reversible triggers, then choose appropriate rate/rhythm strategy and individualise anticoagulation.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Automatically giving an AV-nodal blocker without recognising new hypotension, or automatically anticoagulating immediately after bowel surgery.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: I will check haemodynamic stability first, obtain a 12-lead ECG and call the medical/anaesthetic team for help if unstable.

flow: Assess stability: ABCDE, BP, mentation, chest pain, heart failure and shock.
Confirm irregular narrow-complex AF on ECG and assess triggers: infection, hypoxia, pain, anaemia, fluid status, K/Mg.
In stable AF, discuss rate control, medication contraindications and monitoring with senior/medical team.
Assess stroke risk and bleeding risk, including recent surgery and possible haemostasis concerns, before an individualised anticoagulation decision.
If new haemodynamic instability, urgent senior response and synchronised electrical cardioversion as appropriate; document and arrange monitoring/follow-up.

grid.label: Immediate stability
grid.fail: Starts rate-control drug without checking BP or perfusion.
grid.borderline: Checks pulse only and calls patient stable.
grid.pass: ABCDE, checks BP, consciousness, chest pain, breathlessness and shock.
grid.high: Repeatedly prioritises stability and plans response to any change.

grid.label: ECG diagnosis
grid.pass: Identifies irregular narrow-complex rhythm with absent consistent P waves.
grid.high: Checks for ischaemic changes, rate, and alternative causes.

grid.label: Clinical triggers
grid.pass: Evaluates volume, hypoxia, sepsis, bleeding, drugs, electrolytes.
grid.high: Links low K/Mg to arrhythmia and requests timely correction.

grid.label: Initial investigations
grid.borderline: Bloods only with no ECG plan.
grid.pass: Full observations, ECG, blood count, U&Es/Mg, infection tests as indicated.
grid.high: Targets tests to bleeding, cardiac injury or infection if signs suggest them.

grid.label: Stable management
grid.fail: Gives a poorly chosen agent despite contraindication.
grid.borderline: Says “rate control” but no monitoring or senior plan.
grid.pass: Discusses appropriate rate control with contraindication/EF assessment and review.
grid.high: Clearly separates rate/rhythm choices based on onset, symptoms and physiology.

grid.label: Anticoagulation decision
grid.fail: Starts full-dose anticoagulation (e.g. a DOAC) automatically after surgery without bleeding-risk assessment or surgical input.
grid.pass: Assesses stroke and bleeding risk, recent haemostasis and senior decision on anticoagulation.
grid.high: Explains ongoing reassessment and shared specialist-surgical planning.

grid.label: Deterioration
grid.fail: Gives more oral beta-blocker at BP 76/44.
grid.borderline: Recognises low BP without urgent response.
grid.pass: Recognises unstable AF and calls emergency expert help for synchronised cardioversion.
grid.high: Plans immediate resuscitation, monitoring and cardioversion without delay for anticoagulation.

grid.label: Communication and role
grid.borderline: Tells nurse “doctor will review” without plan.
grid.pass: Escalates to surgical registrar and medical/anaesthetic support, documents actions.
grid.high: Uses concise SBAR and delegates monitoring, medicines and rapid review.

grid.label: Aftercare
grid.pass: Plans repeat ECG, K/Mg and clinical review, discharge follow-up and risk reassessment.
grid.high: Coordinates longer-term AF assessment, stroke prevention and recurrence counselling.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Hello, I am the core surgical trainee. The pulse is fast—perhaps I should give a beta-blocker.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: Nurse: Her pulse is irregular at 142; BP is 118/72.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I do not think we need a 12-lead ECG yet. The rate alone is enough.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: She has just undergone major bowel surgery. What might be contributing?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: It is probably anxiety; no blood tests are necessary.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: What investigations and monitoring do you want?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: None; no bloods or cardiac monitoring are needed.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: Her potassium is 3.2 and magnesium is low.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: That can wait. I will prescribe a rate-control tablet without reviewing contraindications.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: Nurse: She now reports chest pain, looks clammy and BP is 76/44.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Give another tablet and recheck after an hour.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: No one; I will prescribe amiodarone and digoxin myself, and that settles it.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Every postoperative AF patient needs a DOAC immediately, regardless of the operation.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Nothing further; no repeat ECG or follow-up is needed.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I am the core surgical trainee. I will check the patient first: is there chest pain, breathlessness, confusion, hypotension or evidence of heart failure?

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Nurse: She has palpitations but is alert, BP 118/72, saturation 96%, no chest pain now.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Please obtain a 12-lead ECG, attach cardiac monitoring and repeat full observations. The ECG shows an irregular narrow-complex tachycardia, no consistent P waves, rate 142: this is atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: What may have triggered this after a colectomy?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Pain, infection, fluid shifts, hypoxia, blood loss, potassium or magnesium deficits and medication effects. I would examine, review fluid balance, and check FBC, U&Es, magnesium and other tests guided by findings.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Potassium is 3.2 and magnesium 0.61. What next?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Correct electrolytes in a monitored setting, look for bleeding or infection, and discuss rate control with the surgical registrar and medical team, taking account of BP, ventricular function and drug contraindications.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Not automatically. I would assess CHA₂DS₂-VASc stroke risk, ORBIT or bleeding risk, the fresh anastomosis and surgical haemostasis, then make an individualised senior plan. VTE prophylaxis is a separate decision.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Nurse: She now has chest pain, looks clammy, and BP is 76/44.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: She is now haemodynamically unstable. Call the emergency medical/anaesthetic and senior surgical teams, ABCDE, oxygen if needed, IV access and monitoring; prepare urgent synchronised electrical cardioversion. Do not delay life-saving cardioversion to achieve anticoagulation.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: ECG changes, haemodynamics, treatments and response; repeat ECG, electrolytes, recurrence monitoring, stroke/bleeding review and appropriate follow-up.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I will assess this postoperative tachyarrhythmia at the bedside before choosing medication. Nurse, please continue cardiac monitoring and give me repeat BP, mentation, perfusion, oxygenation and any chest discomfort.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Nurse: She is alert and frightened. BP 118/72, pulse 142 irregular, SpO₂ 96% and no chest pain.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: This ECG is irregularly irregular with no discrete consistent P waves and narrow QRS complexes: new AF with rapid ventricular response. I would scrutinise ST segments and verify there is no pre-excitation or alternative arrhythmia.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Where does your diagnostic work begin?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: On the ward and the operation chart: check bleeding, sepsis, pain, urine output, input/output, hypoxia, anaemia, medication, haemoglobin, K and Mg. Order ECG, FBC, U&Es, magnesium and clinically indicated infection or ischaemia tests.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: K is 3.2 and Mg 0.61. How would you manage stable AF?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Correct both deficits appropriately while monitoring ECG and renal function. Discuss rate control with the medical/anaesthetic team, screening for low BP, heart failure, bronchospasm or structural disease before selecting a drug; revisit rhythm control if symptoms persist or the situation changes.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Could you start a DOAC simply because she is 71?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Age contributes to risk, but it does not settle the decision. I will assess formal stroke risk and bleeding risk, determine AF duration, examine whether the anastomosis is haemostatically secure, and agree timing and drug choice with the operating consultant and relevant specialist. We must document reassessment.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Nurse: She has suddenly developed central chest pressure and is sweaty. BP 76/44.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: We have crossed into instability. Activate emergency response now, call senior surgery and anaesthesia, prepare monitored resuscitation and urgent synchronised electrical cardioversion. An unstable patient must not wait for anticoagulation or an oral rate-control tablet.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: “Postoperative day two after right hemicolectomy, new ECG-confirmed AF at 142 initially stable, K 3.2/Mg 0.61, now chest pain and BP 76/44; emergency team and cardioversion preparations underway.”

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Continue rhythm and haemodynamic monitoring, review cause, repeat electrolytes and ECG, assess cardiac function as indicated, and ensure a documented anticoagulation review and follow-up plan even if sinus rhythm returns.

failures.move: Treats BP 76/44 with further oral rate-control medication instead of emergency response.
failures.consequence: Risks collapse and delay to cardioversion.

failures.move: Automatically starts full-dose anticoagulation after major bowel surgery without a bleeding-risk assessment and surgical input (recent surgery affects timing; it does not permanently rule anticoagulation out).

recovery.when: If you focused too early on rate control
recovery.line: I have focused too early on rate control. Let me first repeat the blood pressure and determine whether this is unstable AF before choosing treatment.

recovery.when: When the blood pressure falls to 76/44 with chest pain
recovery.line: The blood pressure has now fallen to 76/44 with chest pain. I must abandon the stable pathway and request immediate cardioversion support.

knowledge.fact: Postoperative AF after non-cardiothoracic surgery is managed as other newly presenting AF.
Correct reversible causes including hypoxia and electrolyte imbalance.
ECG confirmation and initial assessment precede selection of treatment.
Life-threatening instability requires emergency electrical cardioversion without delaying for anticoagulation.
Anticoagulation requires stroke-risk and bleeding-risk assessment, particularly after recent surgery.
Clinical concern and hypotension trigger urgent escalation and increased observation.

recall.think: Stable or unstable AF comes before choosing rate control.
do: Monitor, investigate K/Mg/bleeding/sepsis, involve senior team.
recall.trap: Never medicate through shock or automatically anticoagulate a fresh anastomosis.
recall.finish: Risk-balanced anticoagulation review and follow-up after acute treatment.

reveals.finding: currently no chest pain, syncope or breathlessness; alert, BP 118/72.

reveals.trigger: Later cue, AFTER stable treatment discussion
reveals.finding: “She has just developed chest pain and is clammy; BP now 76/44.”
